title: Electricity in copper
kid: Ethernet sends tiny voltage pushes down twisted copper pairs. The twists help noise cancel out, and the cable can talk both ways at once. After about 100 m the pushes get too faint and smeared. This is how the cable envelope travels.
nerd: 1000BASE-T uses differential signalling on all four Cat 5e pairs. Each pair runs 125 MBd with PAM-5 levels near ±1 V, hybrids and echo cancellation make every pair full duplex, and the standard budgets about 100 m for loss and crosstalk.
extra: Power over Ethernet: a cable like this can carry power too, so an access point or a camera on the ceiling needs no socket. Direct current rides on the pairs as a common-mode (phantom) voltage that the data, sent as differences, never notices: 15.4 W with 802.3af, 30 W with 802.3at, up to 90 W on all four pairs with 802.3bt. Faster copper: 2.5G, 5G and 10GBASE-T use 16 levels instead of 5 (PAM-16, paired into DSQ128 symbols with LDPC error correction). 2.5G and 5G run on ordinary Cat 5e/6; 10G runs 800 MBd per pair and needs Cat 6A for the full 100 m.

describe.kid: Two network boxes sit at the ends of a thick cable. Inside are four twisted pairs. Glowing electric pulses move both ways through the pairs. The cards zoom into the twists, the pulses and the fading after about 100 metres.
describe.nerd: The cable cutaway shows four differential pairs carrying full-duplex pulses between endpoints. Cards show opposite voltages on a twisted pair, PAM-5 levels and an eye diagram. A 100 metre marker shows the channel budget as pulses fade.

manchester.title: Manchester code
manchester.line: A flip in the middle of every bit.

manchester.bothWays: One pair each way, taking turns

1995.kid: Ethernet sends tiny voltage pushes down twisted copper pairs. In 1995 it uses just two of them: one pair to send, one to listen, taking turns. The twists help noise cancel out, and after about 100 m the pushes get too faint.
1995.nerd: 10BASE-T (1990) uses two pairs of a Cat 3 cable: one to send, one to receive, as differential signals at 10 Mbit/s in Manchester code, which flips the line in the middle of every bit so the receiver finds its clock in the data. On a hub only one end talks at a time (half duplex); the other two pairs stay unused.
1995.extra: Before 10BASE-T, Ethernet ran on coaxial cable shared by every computer on it: thick “yellow cable” (10BASE5, 1983) and then thin coax (10BASE2). Twisted pair and a hub in a cupboard made it cheap and easy to wire. Fast Ethernet (100BASE-TX, 1995) was just arriving; gigabit over copper came in 1999.

describe.kid: Two network boxes sit at the ends of a thick cable. Inside are four twisted pairs, but only two glow. A pulse runs along one pair, then another comes back along the other: they take turns. The cards zoom into the twists, the pulses and the fading after about 100 metres.
describe.nerd: The cable cutaway shows four pairs, two of them live: one carries pulses forward, the other back, in turns. Cards show opposite voltages on a twisted pair, a Manchester-coded bit pattern with a flip in every bit, and a two-level eye diagram.

2010.extra: Power over Ethernet: a cable like this can carry power too, so an access point or a camera on the ceiling needs no socket. Direct current rides on the pairs as a common-mode (phantom) voltage that the data, sent as differences, never notices: 15.4 W with 802.3af (2003), and 30 W with 802.3at, new in 2009. Faster copper: 10GBASE-T (2006) uses 16 levels instead of 5 (PAM-16, paired into DSQ128 symbols with LDPC error correction), runs 800 MBd per pair and needs Cat 6A for the full 100 m. In 2010 it was still mostly for servers.
